questions.scenario: A city library system is redesigning how community rooms are booked. Claude analyzed interview notes from branch librarians and from the community-programs team. Branch staff said walk-in groups should always get first claim on any room that is free; the programs team said every room should be reservable online up to 30 days in advance. Claude's draft contains one blended line: "Rooms can be reserved online up to 30 days ahead; walk-ins are accepted when a room is free."
questions.stem: The operations manager will present the requirements to both groups next week and wants the document to be the most reliable basis for their decisions. What should she do?

options.text: Keep the blended requirement, because Claude found wording that covers what both groups asked for in their interviews.
Ask Claude to re-read the notes and confirm it is confident that the blended wording reflects what both groups meant.
Ask Claude to list each conflict explicitly, with quotes from both sources, and take the conflicts to the two groups' leads to decide.
Re-run the analysis with a more capable model so it can reason more deeply and resolve the conflict between the two groups.

questions.explanation: The two rules genuinely conflict: if rooms can be booked a month in advance, walk-ins will often find none free — the opposite of what branch staff asked for — and Claude's blended line hides that conflict. Claude is very good at **surfacing** conflicts with evidence (quotes from each source), but choosing a trade-off between stakeholder groups is a business decision the process owners must make. An explicit conflict list gives both leads something concrete to decide on.

whyWrong.A: A smooth compromise that no stakeholder agreed to looks finished but quietly decides the issue. One group will object later, after work has started.
whyWrong.B: Self-reported confidence is not a reliable accuracy signal, and re-reading does not change the fact that the decision belongs to the stakeholders, not to Claude.
whyWrong.D: A larger model may phrase the compromise better, but the gap is ownership of the decision, not reasoning power.

questions.mindset: Claude surfaces conflicts; stakeholders resolve them.

questions.stem: An HR director has 1,200 anonymized free-text comments from an employee benefits survey, loaded into the company's approved Claude workspace. She needs to know which issues matter most to staff so she can decide what a pilot should cover. Which approach gives her the MOST useful and checkable result?

options.text: Have Claude group the comments into themes with a count for each and two or three verbatim examples, then spot-check a sample against the raw export.
Have Claude write a short executive summary of the top three things employees want, in plain language ready to forward to the leadership team.
Have Claude read all the comments and recommend which benefits changes to make first, ranked by their likely impact on staff retention.
Have Claude rate the survey's overall sentiment from 1 to 10 and explain the main reasons behind the score in a few sentences.

questions.explanation: Themes **with counts and verbatim examples** turn 1,200 comments into a structure the director can trust and check: counts show how widespread each issue is, quotes show what people actually said, and a spot-check of a sample against the raw export catches miscounted or invented themes before decisions are made.

whyWrong.B: A top-three summary drops the counts and quotes, so the director cannot tell how widespread each issue is or verify the summary against the data.
whyWrong.C: This jumps from analysis to a business recommendation and invents a retention-impact ranking that the survey data cannot support.
whyWrong.D: A single sentiment score hides which specific issues people raised, which is exactly what the pilot decision needs.

questions.mindset: Ask for structure plus evidence you can check, not a verdict.

questions.scenario: A university facilities team drafted requirements for a new maintenance-request process: "Requests must be handled quickly", "The request form should be easy to use" and "Urgent issues get priority." The software vendor replied that none of these can be tested.
questions.stem: Which approach fixes the problem MOST effectively with minimal rework?

options.text: Ask Claude to replace each vague phrase with a specific number it judges reasonable for a university facilities team, then send the list to the vendor.
Ask Claude to add more background detail and examples to each requirement so the vendor understands the team's intent more clearly.
Send the vendor the original list with a note asking them to propose their own measurable targets for each item on the list.
Ask Claude to rewrite each item as a testable acceptance criterion, marking where a target value is needed, and have the team set those values.

questions.explanation: Good requirements and success criteria are **specific and measurable**. Claude can quickly restructure vague wording into testable criteria (for example, "urgent requests are acknowledged within __ hours"), but the target values are business commitments. Marking the blanks keeps Claude doing the restructuring while the team sets the numbers.

whyWrong.A: Claude would be inventing service levels the team never agreed to. Numbers that look precise but are guesses are worse than a visible blank.
whyWrong.B: More description does not make a requirement testable. The vendor still has no pass/fail measure.
whyWrong.C: Letting the vendor set the targets hands a business decision to the party being measured and delays the work.

questions.mindset: Claude structures the criteria; the business owns the numbers.

questions.stem: A nonprofit program director pasted notes from a grant-planning brainstorm into Claude and asked for a requirements list for a volunteer-scheduling solution. The list reads well, but it mixes confirmed facts ("we have 140 active volunteers") with ideas nobody has checked ("volunteers will use a mobile app"). She will share it with the board next week. Which TWO actions improve the list the MOST? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite the list in a more formal tone so it reads as a finished document suitable for a board audience.
Ask Claude to label every item as a requirement, a constraint, an assumption or an open question, based on the notes.
Ask Claude to remove any item it is less than 80 percent confident about so only the reliable requirements remain.
Ask Claude to add five more requirements that are typical of volunteer-scheduling tools so the list looks complete.
Turn the assumptions and open questions into a short list to confirm with the volunteer coordinators before the meeting.

questions.explanation: A list that mixes facts and guesses looks finished but isn't. **Labeling** each item shows the board what is known and what is assumed, and **confirming the assumptions with the people who run the process** turns guesses into facts (or removes them) before anyone commits money.

whyWrong.A: A formal tone makes unchecked assumptions look even more authoritative. It changes style, not reliability.
whyWrong.C: Claude's confidence figure is not a reliable accuracy signal, and an unchecked assumption may be important to keep as an open question.
whyWrong.D: Generic requirements from other organizations are not this nonprofit's needs and add more unverified items.

questions.mindset: Separate what is known from what is assumed, then check the assumptions with people.

questions.stem: The office manager at a small accounting firm has listed possible ways to use Claude. Which one is the BEST choice for the firm's first pilot?

options.text: Automatically emailing final tax-filing advice to clients each week, written by Claude from their files.
Drafting summaries of weekly internal staff meetings, which the manager reviews before sending them around.
Deciding which overdue client invoices to write off, based on Claude's reading of payment history.
Answering clients' tax questions directly through a public chat window on the firm's website.

questions.explanation: A good first use case is **frequent, time-consuming, easy to check and low-risk if wrong**. Internal meeting summaries tick every box, and a human reviews them before they circulate, so errors are caught before anyone relies on them.

whyWrong.A: Tax advice sent to clients without review is high-stakes and regulated. Errors reach clients directly.
whyWrong.C: Write-offs are financial judgment calls with real money at stake. Claude can help analyze, but should not decide.
whyWrong.D: An unsupervised public chat giving tax answers puts unreviewed, possibly wrong advice in front of clients.

questions.mindset: Pilot first where work is frequent, checkable and low-risk.

questions.stem: A warehouse supervisor wants Claude to watch the inventory system all day and automatically place reorders whenever stock falls below a set level. He asks you, a business associate, to set this up this week using his Claude chat account. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Use Claude to capture the requirement (stock thresholds, approvals, systems involved) and route it to the developer or architect team as an integration request.
Write a detailed prompt telling Claude to check stock levels every hour and place a purchase order whenever an item drops below its threshold.
Export the inventory spreadsheet each day, paste it into a chat, and have a clerk enter Claude's suggested orders into the purchasing system as-is.
Tell the supervisor that Claude cannot be used for inventory work and recommend the team keep running the current manual process unchanged.

questions.explanation: Watching a live system and taking actions in another system needs an **integration** built and governed by technical colleagues. The associate's value is analyzing the use case: with Claude's help, writing down thresholds, who approves orders and which systems are involved gives the developers a clear specification.

whyWrong.B: A chat prompt cannot give Claude live access to the inventory system or the ability to place orders. A prompt does not fix a missing integration.
whyWrong.C: This removes the purchasing approval and puts unreviewed suggestions straight into a financial system. It is also slow and error-prone.
whyWrong.D: Refusing outright ignores a legitimate need that can be met safely with the right build and controls.

questions.mindset: If the need is live data or automatic actions, write the requirement and hand it to developers.

questions.stem: A product manager and two colleagues on a Claude Team plan will analyze about 30 anonymized customer interview transcripts over the next month. New interviews arrive weekly, and they must tag every transcript with the same set of pain-point categories. Which setup BEST supports consistent analysis across the team?

options.text: Start a fresh chat each week, paste in the newest transcripts and add a short reminder of the tagging categories at the top.
Ask Claude to remember the tagging categories in one long chat and keep adding every new transcript to that same conversation.
Create a shared Project with the tagging rules in its instructions and the transcripts as its knowledge, so everyone works from the same setup.
Have each colleague write their own tagging prompt, then compare the results at the end of the month to see which works best.

questions.explanation: A **Project** keeps instructions and knowledge sources together and applies them to every chat inside it. Shared with the team, it means all three people use the same tagging rules and the same transcripts, which keeps the analysis consistent week after week and avoids re-typing instructions that drift.

whyWrong.A: Re-typed reminders drift from week to week, and earlier transcripts are not available for comparison.
whyWrong.B: One ever-growing chat eventually runs into context limits, and the two colleagues cannot easily work in it.
whyWrong.D: Three different prompts guarantee three inconsistent sets of tags, which defeats the purpose of the analysis.

questions.mindset: Recurring, shared analysis belongs in a Project with fixed instructions and knowledge.

questions.stem: A regional sales VP tells you, "I need an AI dashboard for my team." You are asked to use Claude to help scope the request. What is the BEST first step?

options.text: Ask Claude to design a dashboard layout that shows the ten most common sales metrics used by similar teams.
Ask Claude to build an interactive dashboard Artifact right away so the VP has something concrete to react to.
Ask Claude to list the AI features in popular dashboard tools so the VP can compare the options available.
Ask Claude to help you prepare questions about the decisions the VP must make and what problem prompted the request.

questions.explanation: "I need a dashboard" is a solution, not a requirement. The first step in analysis is to find the **underlying problem and the decisions** the VP needs to support. Claude is good at generating sharp clarifying questions, and the answers become the context for any later design.

whyWrong.A: Generic metrics may not match what the VP actually needs to decide. This designs before understanding the problem.
whyWrong.B: A quick prototype can help later, but building before you know the problem anchors everyone on a guess.
whyWrong.C: Comparing tool features answers "which product?" before anyone knows "for what problem?"

questions.mindset: Turn a requested solution back into the problem before designing anything.

questions.stem: A hospital's patient-transport coordinator used Claude to draft requirements for a new process for requesting porters, based only on interviews with ward nurses. Before finalizing the requirements, which TWO steps MOST reduce the risk of missing important needs? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude which other groups are involved in this process (such as porters, night-shift staff and patients with mobility needs) and what each might need.
Ask Claude to rate its own requirements list for completeness on a scale of 1 to 10 and explain any low-scoring areas.
Add more ward-nurse interview transcripts so Claude has a larger sample to base the requirements on.
Interview or review the draft with representatives of the groups Claude identified before the requirements are finalized.
Ask Claude to rewrite each requirement in more detail so that any gaps in the process become less likely.

questions.explanation: The draft reflects one viewpoint only. Claude is useful for **brainstorming the stakeholder groups and perspectives** that are missing, but only the real people in those groups can confirm what they need. Together these two steps close the gap.

whyWrong.B: A self-rating cannot reveal needs that were never in the input. Claude cannot know what the porters were never asked.
whyWrong.C: More data from the same group reinforces the same blind spot.
whyWrong.E: More detail on the existing requirements does not add the needs of groups that were left out.

questions.mindset: Use Claude to find missing perspectives, then ask the real people.

questions.stem: A school district has drafted a process for students to borrow laptops. The draft covers the normal path well: request, approval, pickup, return at year end. What is the MOST effective way to use Claude to strengthen it before launch?

options.text: Ask Claude to polish the wording of every step so that families find the process clearer and friendlier to follow.
Ask Claude to list edge cases and failure scenarios, such as lost devices or mid-year transfers, and review the list with help-desk staff.
Ask Claude to confirm that the process is complete and covers every situation a student or family could run into.
Ask Claude to write a longer process document with many more steps so that fewer situations are left uncovered.

questions.explanation: Processes usually break at the exceptions, not the normal path. Claude can quickly **stress-test a draft** by listing edge cases and failure scenarios, and the staff who already handle exceptions can confirm which ones are real and how they should be handled.

whyWrong.A: Clearer wording helps families read the process but does nothing for the situations it doesn't handle.
whyWrong.C: Asking Claude to confirm completeness invites a reassuring yes. It is not evidence that the process works.
whyWrong.D: More steps add complexity without targeting the specific cases most likely to go wrong.

questions.mindset: Stress-test the exceptions, and let the people who handle them confirm.

questions.stem: A consultant asked Claude to turn notes from eight client workshops into a requirements list for the client's expense-approval process. One item says the process "must follow the client's three-level approval policy for amounts over $5,000", but the consultant does not remember anyone mentioning such a policy. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Keep the requirement, because a multi-level approval for large expenses sounds like a sensible control for any client.
Delete the whole requirements list and redo the analysis by hand, since one invented item means none can be trusted.
Ask Claude to cite, for each requirement, the workshop note it came from, and to flag any item it cannot trace to a quote.
Ask Claude to explain why it included the requirement, and keep the item if the explanation turns out to be convincing.
Confirm the approval policy with the client's finance owner before the requirement goes into the final deliverable.

questions.explanation: Language models can fabricate specific-looking details such as policy names and dollar thresholds. **Tracing each requirement back to a quote** shows which items are supported by the source material, and **confirming the suspicious item with the person who owns the policy** settles it against an authoritative source.

whyWrong.A: "Sounds sensible" is exactly how hallucinated details get through. A specific threshold and approval count need a source.
whyWrong.B: Throwing everything away is an over-reaction. Traceability shows which items are well supported.
whyWrong.D: A fluent explanation is not proof. Claude can justify an invented detail just as convincingly as a real one.

questions.mindset: Every requirement needs a source; check untraceable specifics with an authority.

questions.stem: A factory safety officer is considering using Claude to translate machine safety instructions into nine languages for factory staff. No one on the safety team reads most of those languages. When scoring this use case, which concern should weigh MOST?

options.text: Nobody on the team can check the translations, and an error in a safety instruction could injure a worker.
Translating nine languages is lengthy work, so the team might reach its usage limits during the project.
The translated instructions would need to be produced as Artifacts rather than as ordinary chat text.
Claude might write the translations in a slightly different tone from the original English instructions.

questions.explanation: When scoring a use case, **verifiability and error impact** come first. Here no one can check the output and a mistake could hurt someone, so the use case needs qualified human reviewers (for example fluent speakers or a professional translation review) before it can go ahead.

whyWrong.B: Usage limits are a practical detail you can plan around. They are not the main risk.
whyWrong.C: The output format is a minor choice and has nothing to do with whether the use case is safe.
whyWrong.D: Tone differences are cosmetic compared with an unchecked error in a safety instruction.

questions.mindset: If nobody can check it and errors cause harm, add qualified review first.

questions.stem: An operations lead used Claude to analyze a proposed use case, and the write-up says the change "will save about 400 staff hours per year." She wants to quote this figure in a funding request to the CFO. What is the MOST appropriate action?

options.text: Include the figure, because Claude calculated it from the team's own description of the current process.
Round the figure down to 300 hours so the estimate is conservative, and include it in the request.
Ask Claude to show its calculation and assumptions, then measure a baseline of current time spent before quoting a number.
Ask a more capable model to produce a more detailed return-on-investment estimate for the same use case.

questions.explanation: Claude's figure rests on assumptions (how often the task happens, how long it takes, how much time is saved). Making those **assumptions visible** shows what needs checking, and a **measured baseline** turns a guess into evidence the CFO can rely on.

whyWrong.A: A description of the process is not a measurement. The figure depends on assumptions nobody has checked.
whyWrong.B: An arbitrary discount is still an unverified number, just a smaller one.
whyWrong.D: A more detailed estimate built on the same unchecked assumptions only looks more convincing.

questions.mindset: Business-case numbers need visible assumptions and a measured baseline.

questions.stem: A school district IT coordinator has a 60-item requirements list for a new learning platform and three vendor proposals, which district policy allows her to upload to the approved Claude workspace. She wants Claude to compare the proposals against the requirements. Which TWO practices make the comparison MOST reliable? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to pick the strongest vendor and summarize the reasons in one paragraph that leadership can read quickly.
Ask for a table with one row per requirement showing each vendor's status (met, partial, not addressed) and the quoted passage behind it.
Ask Claude to fill in gaps where a proposal is silent with what that vendor most likely offers, based on its general reputation.
Have a person check the quoted passages for the requirements that will decide the choice before a vendor is selected.
Ask Claude to give each vendor an overall score out of 100 so the whole comparison fits neatly on a single slide.

questions.explanation: A requirement-by-requirement matrix with **quoted evidence** makes every judgment checkable and shows clearly where a proposal is silent. A **human check of the deciding rows** confirms the quotes are real and correctly read before money is committed.

whyWrong.A: A one-paragraph verdict hides how the decision was reached and hands a procurement decision to Claude.
whyWrong.C: Filling silences with guesses turns "not addressed" into invented claims, which is the error you most need to catch.
whyWrong.E: A single score hides which requirements each vendor misses and cannot be checked against the proposals.

questions.mindset: Compare with evidence per requirement, and have a human check the rows that decide.

questions.stem: A marketing operations lead asked Claude for requirements for a campaign-approval workflow. Claude returned 45 requirements, including AI image generation and multi-language support that nobody mentioned. The budget covers about six weeks of work. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Keep all 45 requirements, because a fuller list now prevents needs from being missed later in the project.
Ask Claude to rank each item as must, should or could against the goal and budget, with the source of each item, and have the sponsor confirm the scope.
Start over with a shorter prompt that tells Claude to produce no more than ten requirements for the new workflow.
Delete every requirement that sounds technical and keep the rest, since the marketing team is not a technical team.

questions.explanation: The list has grown beyond what anyone asked for and what the budget allows. Asking Claude to **prioritize against the stated goal and constraints, with a source for each item**, separates real needs from additions, and the **sponsor** makes the final scope decision.

whyWrong.A: Unrequested features inflate cost and timeline, and a six-week budget cannot cover them all.
whyWrong.C: An arbitrary cap of ten may cut real needs and keep invented ones. It limits length, not relevance.
whyWrong.D: Whether an item sounds technical has nothing to do with whether it is needed.

questions.mindset: Prioritize against the goal and constraints; the sponsor owns the scope.
